The gusle is a single-string bowed instrument of the Dinaric region of the Balkans, in the bowed / wheel-bowed / violin family of chordophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-71. Its body is mostly a wooden soundbox, often of maple, covered with animal skin, and the top of the neck is often carved; the bow hair is horsehair. The player holds the instrument vertically between the knees and touches the string with the left hand without pressing it to the neck, producing harmonics. It usually accompanies singing, and is used for epics and heroic songs; it is an important instrument of the local oral tradition.

起源尚無共識。七世紀拜占庭史家記述斯拉夫人帶入巴爾幹的小型里拉琴，部分研究者認為: There is no agreement on its origin. A seventh-century Byzantine historian describes a small lyre that the Slavs brought into the Balkans, which some researchers connect with the gusle; other scholars argue for an eastern origin, arriving in Europe with Islamic culture in the tenth century. Reliable written records date from the fifteenth century, sixteenth-century travel accounts mention Bosnia and Serbia, and nineteenth- and twentieth-century sources also place it in Montenegro, Croatia and Albania. In 2018 the Serbian gusle was inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage, and in 2025 the Albanian lahuta was inscribed on the list of intangible heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.
